4375.srule: Secondary stress (¯) only in verbs containing a negative affix: on the negative affix when a word-final future suffix carries the primary stress (/punɛ̄nmbí/ 'I will not go'); otherwise on the final syllable, the negative affix carrying the primary (/nonáɬmīn/ 'we didn't eat'). No secondary stress described elsewhere ('one primary stress' per word).

4377.prule: None stated. Nilamba is described as an H/L tone language (Yukawa 1989: acute = high, unmarked = low, with sentence-final falling/rising realisations; Ngwasi 2021: lexical tone nzala 'hunger' vs nzála 'fingers'). 4381.dloc: Part I ch. 3 'Stress', §3.1 and §3.1.1 (A) 'Demarcative Stress in Simple Words', p. 43; §1.4 'The Structure of the Syllable', p. 30; §3.2 'Stress Shifting - Definitive Stress', p. 52 and p. 56; secondary-stress restrictions and clitics p. 44; affixes, reduplication, compounds pp. 45-49; fast speech §3.1.2 pp. 49-52; emphatic stress §3.3 pp. 56-58.
4381.heavy: No weight criterion is named; the rule counts vowels: every vowel is a syllable and long vowels/identical-vowel sequences are 'regarded as consisting of two syllables' (p. 30), so a word-final long vowel takes the primary stress on its first mora, the word's penultimate mora (poo [pó:], kulii [kulí:], letioo [lètió:]), which in syllable terms is stress on a final long-vowelled syllable; a non-final long vowel can carry the stress on its second mora (hoosi [hoó·si]). Extensionally heavy = long vowel (CVV); the language has only (C)V syllables (no codas, p. 30), so closed syllables play no role; vowel quality plays no role.
4381.prule: Primary stress falls 'fixedly on the second-to-last vowel' of the phonological word, every vowel counting as one syllable (all (C)VV sequences, including long vowels, are two syllables, p. 30): i.e. a penultimate-mora rule. A word-final long vowel therefore carries the primary stress on its first half, the word's penultimate mora (poo [pó:], kulii [kulí:], letioo [lètió:]; contrast the definite forms with the stress shifted to the last vowel, poó [poó·], p. 52); a non-final long vowel whose second half is the penultimate vowel is stressed on that second half with Tongan-type breaking (hoosi [hoó·si] or [hoó·ʃi]); otherwise stress is on the penultimate syllable (pato [pá·to], fafine [fafí·ne]). In syllable terms: final syllable if it contains a long vowel, else penult. Monosyllabic words and monosyllabic affixes never form phonological words alone but attach to a neighbour, so the deictics ni/na, person determiners ke/ne, articles te/he and monosyllabic suffixes pull the primary stress one vowel rightward (fale [fá·le] but fale ni [falé·-ni]; nofo but nofo-'i [nofó·-ʔi]); bisyllabic affixes, each member of a compound or base-modifier sequence, and Type I reduplicants form their own phonological words with their own stress. Stated for slow (deliberate) speech; in fast speech non-phrase-final primary stresses reduce to secondary (pp. 49-52).
4381.srule: Secondary stress on every other vowel preceding the primary ('as a basic rule, every other preceding vowel': pasikala [pàsikála], siokaalafi, letioo [lètió:]); it never falls on the second vowel of a long vowel or of a rising VV sequence, nor normally on an inserted /i/ in loans, and then skips to the preceding vowel (tooketaa [tò:ketá:], taaupo'ou, Melipoane, tikisinale); monosyllabic prefixes take it only if the stem's first vowel is unstressed (fè-kúmi).

4393.quote: While Murui and Mɨka have fixed stress position (word-initial) (Wojtylak 2021a–b), Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode appear to have meaningful contrasts between words according to tonal contours ... Romero Cruz 2015a: 74: 'Landaburu y Echeverri (ms. s f.) así como Orjuela (2010) afirman que el nononotá es una lengua tonal.' 4399.prule: Main stress on the lexical stem syllable (Stammsilbe): prefixes are unstressed and reduce (vesábm), derivational/inflectional syllables are weak; in compounds the first stem syllable carries the main stress (Warnkross 1912: 10 via fn. 1500). Loans and a few compounds are stressed on a non-initial syllable (Meschíen 'Maschine', Mesík 'Musik', Tebáck, Motór, Bürgeméister on the head noun, Améisn). Position follows morphological structure (stem vs affix), not syllable count or weight.
4399.srule: Only for compounds: the first stem syllable carries the strong stress; the second stem syllable also carries it only while the word is still felt as a compound (Warnkross 1912: 10, Wolgast, quoted in Köhncke 2011: 271 fn. 1500). Secondary or rhythmic stress in non-compound words is not mentioned in Köhncke 2011, pp. 271-272 (one loan transcribed „ámesìern“ 'amüsieren' with a grave, without comment).

This means that the stressed syllable must be one of the three last syllables in a PrWd. (p. …
4400.dloc: Ch. 4 'Low German stress', pp. 121-154: §4 introduction pp. 121-122; §4.1 p. 123 (second-hand report of Lindow et al. 1998:30; fn. 120); §4.1.5 'General stress pattern' p. 145; §4.2 pp. 145-146 (Table 24); §4.4 'Conclusions on LG stress' p. 154. Tone: p. 4, fn. 88 p. 68, §5.3.4 p. 182.
4400.heavy: Heavy = (C)VC with a lax vowel (word-internal closed syllable, bimoraic); light = (C)V open syllable, including phonetically long/tense vowels and diphthongs ('CV syllables generally count as light. This means that the respective phonetically long vowels are monomoraic', p. 154); superheavy = final CVVC (phonetically overlong tense vowel) or CVCC, whose final C is extrasyllabic, leaving a heavy CVV<C>/CVC<C>; a plain final CVC in polysyllables does not attract stress ('their weight in word-final position basically depends on the segmental context', p. 154); schwa syllables never stressed.
4400.dflt: Antepenult: 'trochaic stress is assigned generally to the rightmost non-final heavy syllable or else to the rightmost non-final sequence of two light syllables' (p. 122); in bisyllables 'As soon as two light syllables... are available, stress surfaces word-initially. The respective foot structure is then (LL)' (p. 145).
4400.prule: Primary word stress falls within the last three syllables of the prosodic word, assigned by moraic trochees from the right: on the penult if it is (C)VC (closed, lax vowel, heavy); if the penult is (C)V (open, light, even with a phonetically long tense vowel or diphthong) stress moves to the antepenult, whether that is (C)VC or (C)V; a superheavy final syllable (CVVC with overlong vowel / CVCC, final C extrasyllabic) takes final stress; schwa syllables are never stressed. CV.CVC bisyllables regularly take penult stress (Table 24 a: tobak, kivt, dorüm); the CV.CVC bisyllables with final stress (Table 24 b: kajüt, kapell, kapun) and loans like sombrero, bikini are Romance loanwords analysed as carrying lexically pre-specified stress (ID-STR) outside the weight rule.
4400.srule: Exists but placement not analysed: Prehn treats secondary stress 'only where necessary' (p. 121) and ignores 'possible secondary stress' in the tableaux (p. 140); the one remark (fn. 127, p. 125) is that 'Alkoven' [ alko n] 'alcove' (CVC.CV.CəC, primary on the antepenult) has secondary stress on the penult rather than the schwa ultima. No general secondary-stress rule.
